summary:
## Node.js Framework Roundup: Key Concepts

This document summarizes the key characteristics of four popular Node.js frameworks: Encore, Hono, Elysia, and NestJS.

### Framework Spectrum

*   **Lightweight to Feature-Rich**: The frameworks can be placed on a spectrum:
    1.  **Hono**: Most lightweight, ideal for edge computing.
    2.  **Elysia**: Lightweight with a focus on ergonomics and type safety.
    3.  **NestJS**: Opinionated and modular, suitable for large applications.
    4.  **Encore**: Most feature-rich with a backend development platform approach.

## Framework Deep Dives

### Encore
*   **Core Idea**: A backend development platform for building robust, type-safe backends in TypeScript.
*   **Performance**: The fastest in the benchmark due to its **Rust runtime**, which offloads I/O from the single-threaded Node.js event loop.
*   **Type Safety**: Offers both runtime and **compile-time type safety**, including for service-to-service calls and infrastructure definitions.
*   **Infrastructure**: Features **infrastructure-as-code** directly in TypeScript and an `encore run` command for automatic local infrastructure setup (databases, pub/sub), eliminating the need for Docker Compose.
*   **Tooling**: Comes with a built-in development dashboard, live tracing, API documentation, and architecture diagrams.
*   **Dependencies**: Zero npm dependencies.

### Hono
*   **Core Idea**: An ultra-lightweight, small, and fast framework originally built for **Cloudflare Workers**.
*   **Multi-Runtime**: Supports multiple JavaScript runtimes like **Node.js, Bun, and Deno** via an adapter system.
*   **Architecture**: Follows a minimalist, middleware-centric approach similar to Express.
*   **Dependencies**: Zero npm dependencies, making it very lean.
> [!TIP]
> Hono is an excellent choice for applications deployed to edge environments or where bundle size is a critical constraint.

### Elysia
*   **Core Idea**: An ergonomic framework for humans, focused on developer experience and end-to-end type safety.
*   **Type Safety**: Uses the **TypeBox** validation library (`t` module) to provide runtime type safety for API handlers.
*   **Tooling**: Simple one-line setup for **Swagger** documentation and has first-party support for **OpenTelemetry**.
*   **Performance**: Very fast, but validation in the JavaScript layer adds some overhead compared to Encore's Rust-based validation.
*   **Deployment**: Recommended deployment is via `bun build`, which compiles the app into a single, standalone binary.

### NestJS
*   **Core Idea**: A highly **opinionated and modular** framework designed for building large-scale, enterprise-level applications.
*   **Architecture**: Enforces a specific structure using abstractions like **Controllers, Providers (Services), and Modules**.
*   **API Design**: Relies heavily on **decorators** for features like dependency injection.
*   **Flexibility**: Runs on top of either **Express** or **Fastify**, which handle the underlying HTTP server logic.
> [!IMPORTANT]
> NestJS has a steeper learning curve compared to the other frameworks discussed. Its rigid structure is a benefit for long-term maintainability in large teams but can be overkill for smaller projects.

## Key Comparisons

### Performance
*   **Winner**: **Encore** is significantly faster due to its **Rust runtime** handling I/O and validation.
*   **Consideration**: Nest's performance is roughly equivalent to Fastify or Express, with a small amount of overhead.

### API Design & Type Safety
*   **Unopinionated Group**: Hono, Elysia, and Encore offer simple, similar APIs for defining endpoints.
*   **Opinionated**: NestJS stands out with its decorator-heavy, class-based, and modular design.
*   **Type Safety Champions**: **Elysia** and **Encore** provide strong end-to-end type safety. **Encore** goes a step further with **compile-time** safety for inter-service communication and infrastructure.

### Deployment & Infrastructure
*   **Automated**: **Encore** is unique with its automatic local infrastructure setup and optional managed cloud platform that can provision infrastructure in your own AWS/GCP account.
*   **Flexible**: **Hono** offers the most deployment options due to its multi-runtime support.
*   **Standard**: **NestJS** follows a standard `nest build` process to compile TypeScript to a JavaScript `dist` folder.
*   **Bundled**: **Elysia** recommends building a single binary with `bun build` for easy deployment.
transcription:
## Introduction to Node.js Frameworks

So, Node.js frameworks, where do we even begin? With so many options out there, it can feel overwhelming choosing the right one for your project. In this video, I will walk you through the hottest frameworks in the Node.js ecosystem right now and break down their strengths, weaknesses, and best use cases for each one of them.

Whether you're looking for speed, scalability, or simplicity, hopefully we will cover it all. And by the end, you'll know exactly which framework is right for you. The frameworks we will be looking at at are Nest, Encore, Hono, and Elysia. Let's dive in.

## The Framework Spectrum: Lightweight vs. Feature-Rich

So on a scale from most lightweight to most feature-rich, I would position the frameworks like this: so going from left to right is Hono, Elysia, Nest, and then Encore.ts. And this doesn't mean that lightweight is bad; it just depends on the needs of your project. The lightweight nature of Hono is actually one of the unique selling points. With just under 13 kilobytes, it's actually perfect for deploying to Cloudflare workers. But Encore, on the other hand, comes with a lot of built-in features like automatic tracing out of the box and local infrastructure.

So let's take a look at each framework, and we're going to start with Encore. But before we do so, I'm curious to know: have you used any of these frameworks? And what are the frameworks that you're reaching for when starting a new project? Please leave a comment under the video to let us know. So...

## Deep Dive: Encore

Encore.ts is a backend development platform with a simple, declarative syntax that aims to make it easier to build robust and type-safe backends with TypeScript. The framework has a lot of built-in tools to make your development experience smoother and performance-wise, it's the fastest framework in this video.

Encore has built-in request validation. The request and response types you define in regular TypeScript are used to validate the request both during compile and runtime. But unlike the other frameworks in this video, the actual validation is done in Rust and not in JavaScript, and that makes the validation really fast, but more on that a bit later.

Encore makes it easy to create and call services. From a code perspective, actually, a service is just another folder in your repo. And when calling an endpoint in a service, it's just like calling a regular function. But the cool part is that under the hood, those function calls get converted to actual HTTP calls.

With Encore, you integrate your infrastructure as type-safe objects in your application code. So creating a database or pub/sub topic just requires a few lines of application code. Encore comes with a built-in development dashboard, and from here you can call your endpoints, sort of like Postman. And each call to your application results in a trace that you can inspect to see the API request, database calls, or the pub/sub message. The local development dashboard also includes automatic API documentation and an always-up-to-date architecture diagram of your system, which is really nice. And I think it's worth mentioning that even though Encore comes with a lot of built-in features, it in itself has zero npm dependencies.

## Deep Dive: Hono

Moving on to Hono. Hono is the creation of Yuki Wada, and he started the project a few years ago because there were no good Node.js frameworks that worked well with Cloudflare workers. But since then, Hono has added support for other runtimes like Node.js, Bun, and Deno. Hono is really small; the `hono/tiny` preset is actually under 13 kilobytes, which makes it really suitable for deploying to Cloudflare workers. And Hono also has zero npm dependencies, which of course is really impressive.

The multi-runtime selling point is actually really interesting, and it's the idea that no matter the JavaScript runtime, you will be able to run Hono. In their repo, they actually have a concept of adapters where you can see the adjustments that they make for each runtime. I think this has been huge for the adoption of Hono and growing the user base. But realistically, for an individual user, you will probably not switch runtimes once you have your app deployed to the cloud.

And even though Hono is lightweight out of the box, it has a bunch of middleware, both first-party and third-party, that you can install to enhance your app. It's the 'add it when you want to use it' approach that got popular with Express. This can work great as long as your app is small, but when your app is larger, maintaining a huge list of dependencies can be frustrating.

## Deep Dive: Elysia

Moving on to Elysia, an ergonomic framework for humans. So I guess all you non-humans out there, look elsewhere.

Elysia, like Encore, is built for TypeScript and also offers type safety inside your API handlers. Knowing what you're working with inside your API handler saves a lot of time, and it's great to not have to litter your code with type checks everywhere. You specify the request types with this 't' module, which is an extension of the TypeBox validation library. But unlike Encore, the validation happens inside the JavaScript layer, which adds some performance overhead.

Adding Swagger documentation only requires one line of code, and Elysia has first-party support for Open Telemetry, which is really nice, I think. So you can easily monitor your app regardless of the platform. And it's really fast, but not the fastest that we'll be testing today.

## Deep Dive: NestJS

Nest comes next. NestJS is a bit different than the other frameworks in this comparison. Encore, Elysia, and Hono try to offer sort of a minimalistic API for creating endpoints and middleware, and you are free to structure your business code however you wish. Nest, on the other hand, is much more opinionated and forces you to structure your code in a certain way. It offers sort of a modular architecture that organizes code into different abstractions like providers, controllers, modules, and middleware.

Nest is designed to make it easier to maintain and develop large applications, I would say. But whether you're a fan of the opinionated structure Nest offers is, at the end of the day, very subjective. I would say that it might be advantageous for large-scale projects where sort of the long-term maintainability is more important than speed and simplicity. But for smaller projects with just a few developers, the added level of abstraction will probably be overkill for most use cases.

The opinionated nature of Nest also brings with it a steeper learning curve compared to Hono, Encore, and Elysia. When using Nest, you can choose to either use Express or Fastify as the underlying HTTP server framework, so all the Nest functionality is actually added on top of that.

## Performance Benchmark Comparison

Performance speed is perhaps not the most important aspect when choosing a framework, but it's also not something that you can ignore. It will impact your app's responsiveness and ultimately your cloud hosting bill. We have benchmarked both without and with request schema validation, and the measurement is requests per second. The names in the parenthesis, these are the request validation libraries used, and Encore has the request validation built-in. Encore is the fastest of all frameworks in our benchmark. And Nest uses Fastify or Express under the hood, so you can expect the performance of a Nest app to be equivalent to this, maybe a bit slower as Nest adds some overhead.

But how can Encore be this much faster? Well, the secret is that Encore uses a Rust runtime, and Rust is fast. Encore.ts actually consists of two parts: a user-facing TypeScript part for defining APIs and infrastructure, and under the hood, it has a multi-threaded runtime written in Rust. The key to the performance boost is to offload as much work as possible from the single-threaded Node.js event loop to the Rust runtime. For example, the Rust runtime handles all input/outputs like accepting HTTP requests or reading from the database. And once the request or database query has been fully processed, then it gets handed over to the Node.js event loop.

## API Design and Type Safety

Hono, Elysia, and Encore are unopinionated when it comes to how you choose to structure your code, and the way you define APIs and middleware are fairly similar between the frameworks. Here is a get endpoint for each framework, and there are, of course, differences, but if we squint, the APIs look fairly similar, at least similar enough for this not to be a deciding factor in my opinion.

But what really makes a difference is being able to rely on type safety when building a robust application. Encore and Elysia offer type-safe APIs, but Encore also offers compile-time type safety when working with infrastructure like pub/sub. And with Encore, you also get compile-time type safety when calling an endpoint in another service. And if you've ever worked in a microservice architecture before, you know how big of a deal that is.

Nest is the one that really sticks out in terms of API design. There are a lot of concepts and abstractions that go into a Nest app. This can be both a good and a bad thing, and it really depends on your preference. But one thing that will be immediately apparent when looking at a Nest app is the use of decorators. Nest relies heavily on decorators, for example, when using dependency injection to inject a service into controllers. Personally, I'm not a big fan of decorators, and I know that I'm not the only one out there.

## Deployment and Infrastructure Management

The last aspect I want to talk about is deployment and infrastructure. All of these frameworks are similar in that they are deployable to all mainstream cloud platforms like DigitalOcean and fly.io or straight to a cloud provider like AWS and GCP.

Encore is unique in that it offers automatic local infrastructure. `encore run` starts your app and spins up all local infrastructure like databases and pub/sub topics so that you can forget about YAML, Docker Compose, and all the usual headaches. And when building your Encore app, you get a runtime configuration where you can supply the configuration needed for connecting to the infrastructure in your cloud. And if you want to get your Encore app in the cloud quickly and don't feel like self-hosting, you can use Encore Cloud. Encore Cloud offers CI/CD and preview environments for pull requests, among other things. And if you want to, Encore Cloud can provision all the needed infrastructure in your own cloud on AWS or GCP. This means that your app is not dependent on any third-party service, and you have full control of all the infrastructure.

Hono sticks out in that it supports a bunch of different runtimes, and you therefore have a lot of options when it comes to deployment. Deploying to Cloudflare workers, Netlify, or AWS Lambda is easy and does not require a lot of configuration.

With Nest, you run the `nest build` command that compiles your TypeScript code into JavaScript, and this process generates a `dist` directory containing the compiled files. That's pretty much it. And you can then use Node.js to run the `dist` folder. The recommended way to deploy an Elysia application is to compile your app into a binary using the `bun build` command. And once the binary is compiled, you no longer need Bun installed on the machine to run the server.

## Conclusion

And that's it. Hopefully you know what framework to reach for in your next project. I've left a few links in the description under this video that you can check out. See you.
